points.title: Database design
points.must: The design-stage plan of the tables, fields, relationships and the type, size, key and validation of every field; its products are the ERD and the data dictionary.

points.title: Place in the life cycle and steps
points.must: Between analysis (requirements specification) and development; used later by testers and for maintenance. Steps: requirements → entities and attributes → relationships → ERD (resolve M:M) → data dictionary → CREATE TABLE.

points.title: Restrictions on the design
points.must: At least three restrictions (DBMS/hardware, volume of data and users, Law on Personal Data, time and budget, existing data), each linked to a consequence for the design.

points.title: Problems of a poor design
points.must: Data stored repeatedly in one table causes update, insertion and deletion anomalies — each explained with an example; a good design stores each fact once and links tables by keys.

points.title: Entity, instance and attribute
points.must: Entity = a thing / person / event about which data is stored (becomes a table); instance = one record; attribute = one property (becomes a field) — with examples.

points.title: Primary and foreign key
points.must: PK uniquely identifies each record; FK is the PK of another table, used to link the tables — with an example (StudentID).

points.title: ERD vs data dictionary
points.must: ERD = diagram of tables and relationships (overview); data dictionary = description of every field (detail for programmers).

points.title: Finding entities and attributes
points.must: Underline the nouns; nouns with their own data and many instances are entities, single values are attributes; attributes atomic (FirstName/Surname), derived values (Age) not stored; worked example.

points.title: Choosing a primary key
points.must: Unique, never empty, does not change, short; natural vs surrogate key; composite key in a link entity; not a name or phone.

points.title: Degrees of relationship
points.must: 1:1, 1:M and M:M, each with an example and how it is implemented (FK on the many side; 1:1 FK in either table; M:M needs a link entity).

points.title: Deciding the degree
points.must: Ask the question in both directions (one A has many B? one B has many A?) for the given scenario — with an example.

points.title: Crow's foot notation
points.must: Sketch: boxes with PK/FK, single bar = one, crow's foot = many, optional circle = zero; read each end from the other entity; labelled lines.

points.title: Resolving M:M with a link entity
points.must: Why M:M cannot be stored (one value per field; Teacher1, Teacher2 = repeating group) and how a link entity with two FKs gives two 1:M relationships; facts about the link (Dose, LoanDate) go in it — e.g. Member–Book via Loan.

points.title: Common mistakes
points.must: At least two: M:M left in the ERD; FK on the one side; crow's foot at the wrong end; a single value made an entity; name as PK; one-direction question.
